Ionized and molecular gas kinematics in a z=1.4z=1.4 star-forming galaxy

H. Übler, R. Genzel, L. J. Tacconi, N. M. Förster Schreiber, R. Neri, A. Contursi, S. Belli, E. J. Nelson, P. Lang, T. T. Shimizu, R. Davies, R. Herrera-Camus, D. Lutz, P. M. Plewa, S. H. Price, K. Schuster, A. Sternberg, K. Tadaki, E. Wisnioski, S. Wuyts Alternate Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für extraterrestrische Physik, Gießenbachstr. 1, D-85748 Garching, Germany (hannah@mpe.mpg.de) Alternate Affiliation: Departments of Physics and Astronomy, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA Alternate Affiliation: Institut de Radioastronomie Millimétrique, 300 rue de la Piscine, F-38406 Saint Martin d’Hères, France Alternate Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für Astronomie, Königstuhl 17, D-69117 Heidelberg, Germany Alternate Affiliation: Raymond & Beverly Sackler School of Physics & Astronomy, Tel Aviv University, Ramat Aviv 69978, Israel Alternate Affiliation: Center for Computational Astrophysics, Flatiron Institute, 162 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Alternate Affiliation: National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, 2-21-1 Osawa, Mitaka, Tokyo 181-8588, Japan Alternate Affiliation: Research School of Astronomy & Astrophysics, Australian National University, Canberra, ACT-2611, Australia Alternate Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Bath, Claverton Down, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Abstract

We present deep observations of a z=1.4z=1.4 massive, star-forming galaxy in molecular and ionized gas at comparable spatial resolution (CO 3-2, NOEMA; Hα\alpha, LBT). The kinematic tracers agree well, indicating that both gas phases are subject to the same gravitational potential and physical processes affecting the gas dynamics. We combine the one-dimensional velocity and velocity dispersion profiles in CO and Hα\alpha to forward-model the galaxy in a Bayesian framework, combining a thick exponential disk, a bulge, and a dark matter halo. We determine the dynamical support due to baryons and dark matter, and find a dark matter fraction within one effective radius of fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)=0.18−0.04+0.06R_{e})=0.18^{+0.06}_{-0.04}. Our result strengthens the evidence for strong baryon-dominance on galactic scales of massive z∼1−3z\sim 1-3 star-forming galaxies recently found based on ionized gas kinematics alone.

Keywords: 
galaxies: evolution — galaxies: high-redshift — galaxies: kinematics and dynamics

I Introduction

Our knowledge of the kinematics of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at z=1−3z=1-3 is dominated by large surveys targeting ionized gas emission [19, 26, 48, 38, 41, e.g.]. There is strong evidence that the ionized gas kinematics of massive, high-redshift SFGs are dominated by ordered disk rotation, but a key question remains: how do the ionized gas kinematics, particularly the rotation curve and intrinsic velocity dispersion, compare to that of neutral or molecular gas, which dominate the gas mass budget?

Multi-phase, spatially-resolved data exist only for a handful of high-redshift SFGs, where the kinematics of the different gas phases are found to agree [9, e.g.], or not (39, e.g. vs. 33). Yet, deeper data are generally needed for at least one of the gas phases in these studies to compare the kinematics in detail, and to disentangle the contributions from baryons and dark matter. [20] showed through deep integrations of a z=1.5z=1.5 galaxy that its kinematics in Hα\alpha and CO(3-2) agree. However, this galaxy is undergoing a minor merger and is therefore not optimally suited to kinematically analyze the galaxy’s baryon vs. dark matter content.

In this Letter, we analyze the Hα\alpha and CO(3-2) kinematics of a massive SFG at z=1.4z=1.4, EGS4-24985. We have obtained deep data, 21 and 45hrs on source, with the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) and the NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA), making this an unprecedented data set of two important tracers of the gas kinematics in an SFG. We model the galaxy by combining a thick exponential disk, a bulge, and an NFW [31] halo, using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. We discuss correlations among the model parameters and constrain the galaxy’s dark matter fraction within one effective radius (ReR_{e}). Throughout, we adopt a [8] initial mass function and a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology with H0=70H_{0}=70kms-1Mpc-1, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7, and Ωm=0.3\Omega_{m}=0.3.

II Data

II.1 Physical Properties of EGS4-24985

EGS4-24985 (R.A. 14h19m26.66s, Dec. +52∘51′17.0″{}^{\circ}51^{\prime}17.0\arcsec) is a z=1.4z=1.4 galaxy with a stellar mass of M⋆=7.4×1010​M⊙M_{\star}=7.4\times 10^{10}M_{\odot} and a star formation rate of SFR=98.8​M⊙​yr−198.8M_{\odot}{\rm yr}^{-1} [49, both derived following the techniques outlined by], placing it in the upper half of the main sequence at this redshift [47]. The V−,I−,H−V-,I-,H-band ACS and WFC3 images reveal strong spatial color variations, indicative of a mixture of stellar populations, or varying dust obscuration that potentially hides a central mass concentration (Figure 1, left).

The morphological position angle PAH=18∘{}_{H}=18^{\circ}, minor-to-major axis ratio qH=0.60q_{H}=0.60, Re,H=0​.′′​52=4.4R_{e,H}=0\farcs 52=4.4kpc, and Sérsic index nS,H=0.74n_{S,H}=0.74 are constrained from galfit [34] Sérsic models based on the 3D-HST team [37] version of CANDELS HH-band (F160W) imaging [23, 25], presented by [44]. Assuming a ratio of scale height to scale length of q0=0.2q_{0}=0.2, typical for SFGs at this redshift [45, e.g.], the estimated inclination is i=55∘i=55^{\circ}. There is a systematic change in qq as derived from other filters, q=0.54−0.66q=0.54-0.66 from F125W (JJ-band) to F814W (II-band).

Assuming a bulge-to-disk decomposition with nS,disk=1n_{S,\rm disk}=1, nS,bulge=4n_{S,\rm bulge}=4, we infer the bulge-to-total fraction from the stellar mass map to be B/T=0.13±0.15B/T=0.13\pm 0.15 [27].

II.2 CO observations with NOEMA

To explore the kinematics of the cold gas, we observed the CO(3-2) line with the IRAM interferometer NOEMA. At the redshift of the source, the CO(3-2) line (rest frequency 345.796GHz) is shifted into the 2mm band. We observed EGS4-24985 in the D (compact) and A (extended) configurations with 7 or 8 antennas between November 2016 and April 2017. The total equivalent 8-antenna on-source integration time was 45hrs in the D+A configuration, with a resolution of 0​.′′​6−1​.′′​00\farcs 6-1\farcs 0. Weather conditions during the observing periods were excellent, with typical system temperatures of ∼\sim150K. The WiDEX spectral correlator provided 4GHz of bandwidth per polarization with a fixed channel spacing of 2MHz. For phase and amplitude calibration, every 20 minutes we alternated source observations with observations of a bright quasar within 15∘15^{\circ} of the source. The absolute flux calibration was done through bootstrapping from observations of LkHA-101 and MWC-349 (0.36Jy and 1.45Jy at 144GHz), resulting in a continuum flux of 70​μ70\muJy.

The data were calibrated using the CLIC package of the IRAM GILDAS11 1 http://www.iram.fr/IRAMFR/GILDAS software environment, and imaged and analyzed with the MAPPING routines in GILDAS. We applied a uniform weighting scheme to create the data cube, and then subtracted the 2mm continuum emission using channels free of line emission. The final cube was CLEANED with the CLARK version of CLEAN implemented in GILDAS, and reconstructed with a 0​.′′​67×0​.′′​550\farcs 67\times 0\farcs 55 (PA=62∘) clean beam (Figure 1, middle), to a spectral resolution of 19kms-1 with an rms noise of 0.2mJy channel-1synthesized beam-1.

The molecular gas mass as measured from the CO(3-2) flux and using the α\alpha(CO) conversion function by [21] is Mmol=6.9×1010​M⊙M_{\rm mol}=6.9\times 10^{10}M_{\odot}. With a gas-to-baryonic mass fraction of Mmol/Mbar=0.48M_{\rm mol}/M_{\rm bar}=0.48, the galaxy is typical when compared to larger samples at the same redshift [40]. The CO distribution has an approximate extent of Re,CO≈0​.′′​26R_{e,{\rm CO}}\approx 0\farcs 26 (measured from an exponential disk fit in the UV plane). The CO position-velocity (PV) diagram is shown in Figure 1 (right, white contours).

II.3 Hα\alpha observations with LUCI at LBT

We obtained seeing-limited near-infrared spectroscopy of EGS4-24985 using the LUCI1 and LUCI2 spectrographs in binocular mode [6], mounted at the Bent Gregorian focus of the two 8.4m mirrors of the LBT [24]. The observations were carried out over five nights in March 2017, in clear weather or thin clouds, with seeing 0​.′′​6−1​.′′​00\farcs 6-1\farcs 0. We used a pixel scale of 0​.′′​250\farcs 25, the 210 grating in H−H-band and a slit width of 1​.′′​01\farcs 0, yielding a spectral resolution of R∼3000R\sim 3000. We adopted a two-point dithering pattern and an exposure time of 5min per frame, for a total on-source time of 21hrs (summed from both spectrographs). To facilitate acquisition, we used a multi-object mask and chose PA=20∘=20^{\circ} to align the slit to the major axis of the galaxy (§II.1). The data were reduced using the flame pipeline [3], which outputs a rectified, sky-subtracted, wavelength-calibrated two-dimensional (2D) spectrum. The corresponding Hα\alpha PV diagram is shown in Figure 1 (right, color scale).

II.4 One-dimensional kinematic profiles

To create the one-dimensional (1D) velocity and dispersion profiles in CO, we proceed as described by [22]: we first fit a Gaussian profile to the CO line emission in each spaxel of the data cube, smoothed over three spaxels to ensure sufficient S/NS/N in the outer parts of the galaxy. Accounting for the galaxy’s systemic velocity, this results in the 2D velocity map. From this we determine PAkin=23∘{}_{\rm kin}=23^{\circ} as the axis with the steepest velocity gradient. It agrees with PAH, and with the PA of the Hα\alpha slit observations (§§II.1, II.3). The CO 1D velocity and dispersion profiles are then constructed from 0​.′′​750\farcs 75 diameter apertures (as a compromise between the CO data resolution and the seeing-limited Hα\alpha data) with the center spaced by 0​.′′​240\farcs 24 along PAkin.

To create the 1D profiles in Hα\alpha, we extract spectra in overlapping bins of two to four spatial pixels and fit a Gaussian profile to the Hα\alpha line emission. The choice of the number of spatial pixels used for the extraction of individual data points does not substantially affect the extracted values, but allows for increased S/NS/N in the outer disk regions.

We trace Hα\alpha out to 19kpc (NE, ∼4.4​Re,H\sim 4.4R_{e,H}) and 13kpc (SW, ∼3.1​Re,H\sim 3.1R_{e,H}), and CO out to 12kpc (∼2.8​Re,H\sim 2.8R_{e,H}). These physical radii at z∼1.4z\sim 1.4 are equivalent to probing the rotation curve out to 23-35kpc for a galaxy of this stellar mass at z∼0z\sim 0 [45]. Figure 2 shows the 1D velocity and dispersion profiles in CO and Hα\alpha along PAkin in observed space. The uncertainties are derived from the Gaussian fits described above where noise has been taken into account. The two tracers agree, indicating that they trace the same mass distribution, most reliably in the outer disk where beam-smearing effects become less important.

The galaxy’s intrinsic velocity dispersion, ∼\sim15-30kms-1, is at the lower end of typical values of SFGs at this redshift (∼\sim45kms-1; 48; see also 15). This is evident from the outer regions of the 1D profile, where, under the assumption of constant intrinsic velocity dispersion, the effect of beam-smearing on the measured dispersion is low. Therefore, in the case of EGS4-24985, the correction for pressure support from the turbulent gas motions to the circular velocity is small (∼\sim8kms-1 at 2​.′′​32\farcs 3), and thus does not lead to a significant drop in the observed outer rotation curve. Considering the limitations of the instrumental spectral resolution, the recovered dispersion values represent upper limits.

III Modelling

Since the 1D kinematic profiles of ionized and molecular gas agree within their uncertainties, it is justified to combine them to improve constraints on our model parameters. We have also separately analyzed the Hα\alpha and CO data and found agreement of the results within the uncertainties (Table 1).

The kinematic modelling of our galaxy follows the methodology described by [50] and [22]. We build a mass model consisting of a thick exponential disk (nS=1n_{S}=1, q0=0.2q_{0}=0.2) a bulge (nS=4n_{S}=4, q0=1q_{0}=1, Re=1R_{e}=1kpc), and an NFW halo. We fit the mass model simultaneously to the 1D velocity and dispersion profiles of Hα\alpha+CO along PAkin. For the baryonic mass distribution, we account for a finite flattening following [32]. Our choice of an nS=1n_{S}=1 disk plus bulge is motivated by the bulge-to-disk decomposition and the likely high dust obscuration in the center of the galaxy.

The modelling uses an updated version of dysmal [10, 12, 50]. This code accounts for spectral and spatial beam-smearing, and incorporates the effects of pressure support on the circular velocity from the turbulent gas motions of the kinematic tracer, as described by [4] and [50] [see also 11, for a detailed discussion]. The most important update to dysmal consists of the implementation of an MCMC sampling procedure using the emcee package [18]. A full description of the updated code will be presented by Shimizu et al. (in prep.).

Free parameters in our modelling are MbarM_{\rm bar}, ReR_{e}, B/TB/T, ii, σ0\sigma_{0}, and the NFW halo mass MhaloM_{\rm halo}. We choose the prior halo mass to be typical for the redshift and stellar mass of our galaxy [30]. The concentration parameter is fixed to a value typical for this halo mass and redshift, c=4.4c=4.4 [17]. We verify that the typical concentration parameters for the range of halo masses derived from the MCMC sampling are broadly consistent with this value (Δ​c∼0.2\Delta c\sim 0.2 for the 1σ\sigma distribution of sampled halo masses). We explore setups with lower/higher concentrations (c=2;8c=2;8), and consequently find lower/higher fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)R_{e}) and higher/lower MhaloM_{\rm halo}, consistent with our main results (Table 1). We do not consider adiabatic contraction since its net effect at high redshifts is not well constrained [16, e.g.].

In calculating the model likelihood, we assume Gaussian measurement noise. For the purpose of parameter inference, we choose Gaussian priors for all model parameters that reflect our prior state of knowledge about their values and uncertainties (Table 1). As discussed in §II.1, qq and ReR_{e} are independently constrained through galfit models. The adopted uncertainties of σi=10∘\sigma_{i}=10^{\circ} and σRe=0​.′′​10\sigma_{R_{e}}=0\farcs 10 are conservative estimates [44, see]. Through our choice of narrow Gaussian priors for these parameters, we translate their uncertainties directly into the modelling. We choose B/T=0.2B/T=0.2 with σB/T=0.15\sigma_{B/T}=0.15 to account for a possible bulge hidden by dust extinction. For MbarM_{\rm bar} and MhaloM_{\rm halo}, we adopt uncertainties of ∼50%\sim 50\%. For σ0\sigma_{0}, our estimate is roughly based on the outer values of the dispersion profile. If we adopt flat priors for MhaloM_{\rm halo} and B/TB/T, we find consistent results. We also explored a model with fixed stellar and gaseous exponential disks, no bulge, free σ0\sigma_{0}, MhaloM_{\rm halo}, and cc, leading to a central dark matter fraction of <1%<1\% (Table 1).

For our fiducial model, we set up the MCMC sampling of the posterior probability function of the parameters with 180 walkers, a burn-in phase of 500 steps, and a running phase of 2000 steps. The length of the burn-in was designed to ensure convergence of the chains, while the length of the final run was designed to be >10 times the maximum autocorrelation time of the individual parameters. The acceptance fraction of the final run was 0.35.

IV Results

IV.1 Parameter correlations and fiducial model

The MCMC sampling of the joint posterior probability distributions of the model parameters is visualized in the top rows of Figure 3. The median values and 1σ\sigma confidence ranges of the marginalized distributions are indicated by the dashed vertical lines in the 1D histograms (see also second column in Table 1).

For the 2D marginalized distributions, contours show the 1σ\sigma, 2σ\sigma, and 3σ\sigma confidence levels. The strongest correlation is between inclination and MbarM_{\rm bar}. This is expected, since any inclination correction to the observed rotation velocity directly affects the inferred dynamical mass. This is also reflected to a smaller extent in the correlation between inclination and MhaloM_{\rm halo}.

Since the posterior distribution is well behaved, we choose our fiducial model to be represented by the median values of the individual marginalized distributions, with uncertainties represented by the 1σ\sigma confidence ranges. The median values are also shown as blue squares in the 2D histograms in Figure 3. Every median lies close to the mode of the posterior distribution in projection, indicating that they lie in the most likely parameter space.

The 1D profiles of velocity and dispersion corresponding to the fiducial model in observed space are shown as grey lines in Figure 2.

IV.2 Central dark matter fraction

We measure the enclosed dark matter fraction at ReR_{e} from the intrinsic properties of the dysmal model defined by the median sampling results, and find fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqReR_{e}=OPEN0​.′′​49)=vDM2​(Re)/vcirc2​(Re)=0.200\farcs 49)=v_{\rm DM}^{2}(R_{e})/v_{\rm circ}^{2}(R_{e})=0.20. vDMv_{\rm DM} is the contribution to the circular velocity of the dark matter halo, and vcircv_{\rm circ} is the total circular velocity. The galaxy is strongly baryon-dominated within ReR_{e}. This baryon-dominance prevails out to r=1​.′′​46r=1\farcs 46 (3​Re3R_{e}). Our model agrees with the baryonic disk being ‘maximal’, vdisk​(Rmax)/vcirc​(Rmax)=0.90v_{\rm disk}(R_{\rm max})/v_{\rm circ}(R_{\rm max})=0.90, where Rmax=0​.′′​44R_{\rm max}=0\farcs 44 is the radius where the disk velocity reaches its peak value [43, e.g.]. The intrinsic model rotation curve and mass component curves are shown in Figure 4. The inferred baryon-to-total mass fraction md=0.03m_{d}=0.03 is compatible with predictions from abundance matching estimates that account for gas mass [5].

Through the MCMC sampling, we also gather information on the probability distribution of fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)R_{e}), which is not itself a model parameter but calculated from the intrinsic models. In Figure 3 (bottom row) we show the 1D and 2D histograms of the marginalized posterior distribution of the fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)R_{e}) values associated with the sampled parameter space. While correlations with some of the model parameters are evident, particularly with MbarM_{\rm bar} and with the structural parameters ReR_{e} and B/TB/T, dark matter is sub-dominant within ReR_{e} for the explored parameter space. We use the median and 1σ\sigma confidence ranges of the marginalized probability distribution to estimate fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)R_{e}) and its uncertainties, and find fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)=0.18−0.04+0.06R_{e})=0.18^{+0.06}_{-0.04}.

V Discussion & Conclusions

We have presented kinematic data of a z=1.4z=1.4 SFG based on independent and deep Hα\alpha and CO(3-2) observations. We find that the ionized and molecular gas trace the same gravitational potential, as their kinematics agree within the uncertainties. Thus, we combine them to model the galaxy.

We use MCMC sampling to constrain a mass model consisting of a thick exponential disk, a bulge, and an NFW halo. We find that the galaxy’s central region is baryon-dominated with a dark matter fraction of fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)=0.18−0.04+0.06R_{e})=0.18^{+0.06}_{-0.04}. This is in agreement with recent findings of low central dark matter fractions in high-redshift SFGs by several groups [19, 46, 1, 36, 38, 50, 22, 28].

Together with vcirc​(Re)=296v_{\rm{circ}}(R_{e})=296kms-1, this places EGS4-24985 into the same region of the vcircv_{\rm circ}-fDMf_{\rm{DM}} parameter space as the two z∼1.5−1.6z\sim 1.5-1.6 galaxies observed in Hα\alpha by [22] – a region also populated by massive local SFGs [35, 2, 13, 29, e.g.] and early-type galaxies [7, e.g.]. The latter are the likely descendants of massive SFGs at z∼1−3z\sim 1-3. Our result supports the interpretation by [22] that the low central dark matter fractions observed during the peak epoch of cosmic star formation rate density might be preserved over the rest of cosmic history, as massive SFGs quench and evolve into passive galaxies. Also, this suggests that massive disks are baryon-dominated in their centers at all times.

The low pressure support in our galaxy results in a flat intrinsic rotation curve despite the low fDM​(≤CLOSEf_{\rm DM}(\leqOPENRe)R_{e}), thus setting it apart from the galaxies presented by [22]. It also implies that in this case the slope of the rotation curve in the outer disk region is a closer tracer of the relative contributions of baryons and dark matter to the rotational support of the galaxy. The low intrinsic dispersion further suggests that the galaxy is more settled than other galaxies at this redshift with otherwise comparable physical properties [22], indicating that any potential dissipative condensation has happened at earlier times [14, e.g.]. Still, EGS4-24985 falls on the high-redshift Tully-Fisher relations [42].

The agreement of the deep Hα\alpha and CO data especially in the outer disk helps to alleviate concerns that ionized gas kinematics at high redshift might be unrepresentative of the galaxy kinematics, and could instead be circum-galactic or in-/outflowing gas in disguise. Future studies with high-quality resolved kinematics traced through multiple gas phases in SFGs at similar redshifts will be important to statistically corroborate our result.

We are grateful to the anonymous referee for a constructive report that helped to improve this manuscript. We thank the staff at IRAM and LBT for their helpful support with the NOEMA and LUCI observations for this work.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
